levels.title: Twenty Questions
levels.story: Fenn stands at the gate with a chalkboard. "Do I water the field today? I ask myself a few questions: is the soil dry, is it raining. A computer can build that list of questions from my old notes, if I tell it which question to ask first."

everyday.scene: A doctor's clinic asks you a few questions at the desk, and each answer decides what question comes next. A flowchart on the wall guides the staff.
everyday.question: How can a computer build a list of questions like that from old records?
everyday.answer: It tries each question on the records, keeps the one that sorts the answers best, and repeats inside each group. The result is a decision tree.

lessons.title: A tree of questions
text: A decision tree is a chain of yes-or-no style questions. Each answer sends an example down a branch. At the end of a branch is a leaf, which gives the prediction.
The table is Fenn's ten past days, with the answer in the last column: was it right to water? The best first question is not obvious by eye, and a computer can score every question.

terms.meaning: The end of a branch, where the tree gives its answer.
A question that divides the examples into groups.

lessons.title: Pure groups
text: A good question makes each group less mixed. A group that is all Yes or all No is pure. Entropy measures how mixed a group is: 0 for pure, and 1 for an even split between two classes.

Information gain is the entropy before a split minus the weighted average entropy after it. The question with the biggest gain goes first. The ten days start at 0.97. The table shows the gain for each question.

predict.prompt: Which question should go at the top of the tree?
predict.answer: Soil, because it has the biggest gain.

lessons.title: Grow, then stop
text: After the first split, the same method runs inside each group. Here the damp group is already pure. The dry group still has one No, so a second question about rain finishes the job.
A tree allowed to grow without limit can end up with a leaf for nearly every example. That memorises noise, which is called overfitting. Limits such as a maximum depth keep trees simple.

text.text: Many tree builders use Gini impurity instead of entropy. It is another way to score how mixed a group is, and the CART algorithm uses it for classification trees.

activities.prompt: Five of Fenn's days were Yes and five were No. What is the entropy of that group? (0 means pure, 1 means an even split.)
hints: An even split between two classes is the most mixed it can be.
The entropy is the top of the scale.
activities.explain: An even split of two classes has entropy 1, the most mixed possible.

activities.prompt: Which question gives the biggest information gain on Fenn's ten days?
hints: Check the gain table.
Soil is 0.61. The others are lower.
activities.explain: Soil has the biggest gain, 0.61. Wind has only 0.05 because windy and calm days are about equally mixed.

activities.prompt: Walk a new day down the tree.
activities.explain: Each question narrows the options until a leaf gives the answer. This day had dry soil and no rain, so the tree says water.

state.legend: Left of a question: damp soil or rain. Right: dry soil or no rain.

steps.say: This is the finished tree. A new day arrives: dry soil and a cloudy sky. Follow the questions down from the top.

hints: Damp soil goes left to a leaf. Dry soil needs one more question.
Dry means the day carries on to Rain?.

state.legend: Left of a question: damp soil or rain. Right: dry soil or no rain.

steps.say: The second question asks about rain. The sky is cloudy, not rainy.

hints: Only a rainy day goes left, to No.
Cloudy is not rainy, so it goes right.

steps.say: The day reaches a leaf. The tree says Yes: water the field.

activities.prompt: Is each group pure or mixed?
hints: Pure means every example has the same label.
Any group with both labels is mixed.
activities.explain: Pure groups have only one label. Groups with both labels are mixed, even if one label is rare.

activities.prompt: After asking about soil, the damp group has 5 days and all of them are No. What is its entropy?
hints: Is the group pure?
A pure group has no mixing.
activities.explain: A group where every day is No is pure, so its entropy is 0.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of growing a tree in order.
items: Score every question on the current group
Stop when groups are pure or a limit is reached
hints: Score before you split.
Stopping comes last.
activities.explain: Score the questions, split on the best, repeat inside each group, and stop at pure groups or a limit.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: Where a branch ends in a prediction
How much a split reduces mixing

hints: Entropy is about one group, gain about a split.
A leaf is the end of a path.
activities.explain: Leaves predict, splits divide, entropy measures mixing, and gain measures how much a split helps.

activities.prompt: Why limit how deep a tree can grow?

options.text: A tree with a leaf for almost every example memorises noise

hints: What happens if every example gets its own leaf?
That fits the training days perfectly but may fail on new days.
activities.explain: An unlimited tree can fit noise in the training data. That is overfitting, so depth is limited.

activities.prompt: In the tree from the simulation, how many leaves are there?
hints: A leaf has no questions below it.
The two Rain? answers give two leaves, and the damp soil answer gives one.
activities.explain: The tree has three leaves: Damp gives No, rainy gives No, and not rainy gives Yes.

activities.prompt: Challenge: after asking about soil, the damp group (5 days) has entropy 0 and the dry group (5 days) has entropy 0.72. What is the weighted average entropy after the split?
hints: Each group is half of the days.
activities.explain: Half the days are in each group, so the weighted entropy is 0.5 x 0 + 0.5 x 0.72, about 0.36. The gain is 0.97 - 0.36 = 0.61.

activities.prompt: Challenge: why is Wind a poor first question for these days?

options.text: Windy and calm days are both a mix of Yes and No

hints: Look at the gain: it is only 0.05.
A question helps only if it makes groups purer.
activities.explain: Splitting on wind leaves both groups about as mixed as before, so the gain is tiny.

feed.prompt: What is the entropy of a pure group?
feed.explain: A group with a single label has no mixing, so its entropy is 0.

feed.prompt: Which question goes first in a decision tree?

options.text: The one with the biggest information gain
The one that is asked the most often
The first column of the table

feed.explain: The first split is the one that reduces mixing the most.

feed.prompt: Why can a very deep tree do badly on new data?

options.text: It memorised noise in the training data

feed.explain: Overfitting means fitting noise, which does not repeat in new data.

feed.prompt: A group has 6 Yes and 0 No. What is its entropy?

fieldNotes.title: Entropy and trees
fieldNotes.text: Decision tree builders such as ID3, C4.5 and C5.0 use information gain, which is based on entropy, to choose splits.

fieldNotes.title: Overfitting in trees
fieldNotes.text: scikit-learn's guide says decision-tree learners can create over-complex trees that do not generalise well, and suggests limits such as a maximum depth.

summary: You scored questions by entropy and information gain, put the best one at the top, and watched a tree turn a new day into a Yes or a No.
Fenn chalks the three leaves on the gate. "Three answers, two questions."

mistake.title: Asking the question that sounds sensible instead of scoring it
mistake.text: A tree builder tries every question and keeps the one that makes groups purest. A question can sound useful and still barely help.
